Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, well, it’s kind of a lot, to be honest. I’m here because... well, I’m taking some college classes right now and doing my clinicals—I'm training to be a radiologic technologist. And the thing is, I just feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin almost all the time. I just can't do it. 

I really have been trying to just tough it out, you know? For months now, I keep telling myself, 'Just sit in the chair, just be quiet, stop moving,' but the feeling just builds and builds inside me until it's completely unbearable. I always end up pacing around the control room, or shifting my weight constantly in my seat, or I have to invent some random excuse to get up and move. Like, I'll pretend I need to go check the inventory in the supply closet, or I'll go to the bathroom when I don't even have to go, just so I can walk down the hallway for a minute. It’s just this constant, intense need to be doing something physically, and it's making my classes and my time in the clinic really, really frustrating.

No, honestly, paying attention really isn't the problem at all. It’s kind of weird because I think people assume that since I’m always moving around or looking restless, I must not be listening, but I actually hear everything. Like, in my anatomy and physiology lecture—it's a three-hour block, which is just agonizing—I know exactly what the professor is saying. My brain is totally tracking the information. I wasn’t distracted or forgetting what step came next. I just... I literally couldn't keep my feet planted on the floor. I was bouncing on my heels, tapping my hands against my lead apron, shifting my weight back and forth. The supervising tech even asked me if I was lost or confused, but I wasn't lost at all! I could recite the exact protocol we were doing right back to him. 

It’s not my brain wandering off, you know? It’s just my body refusing to stay in standby mode. So, yeah, I really don't think it's an attention thing. I absorb the material just fine when I'm looking at the imaging screens or listening to a lecture, I just absolutely have to be in motion while I'm doing it.

Emotions? Like... getting happy or sad or something? Um, I don't really think so. I mean, honestly, the need to move is just... it's just always there, you know? It's not like I get suddenly really stressed out about a difficult patient or an upcoming exam and then suddenly I have to start pacing. And then, before I even realized what I was doing, I stood up and started pacing around the breakroom while I finished my sandwich. I wasn't upset or anything! I was just... eating. 

And it's the same way when I'm studying. I could be reviewing something super straightforward, like basic anatomy of the hand—you know, the carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, stuff I've known forever and I'm not worried about at all—and I'll still be shifting in my chair constantly, crossing and uncrossing my legs, standing up to stretch every five minutes. It doesn't matter if I'm feeling calm, or happy, or annoyed, or whatever. The physical energy is just... there. It's like a motor that's always running, regardless of what's going on in my head emotionally. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't tie it to any specific emotion. It's just my normal state of being. I mean, maybe if I get really, really excited about something, like if I nail a perfect lateral lumbar spine x-ray on the first try without having to repeat it, maybe I'll jump around a little more than usual, but even then, it's just an amplification of what's already happening, not a new thing triggered by the excitement, if that makes sense. It's just a constant, physical need to not be still.

Well, I haven't exactly stopped doing things on purpose, but... I mean, things are definitely being forced to change right now, especially with my schooling. Like, my clinical evaluations? They have absolutely taken a massive hit recently, which is... it's just really bad. 

Because, you see, in the rad tech program, clinicals are basically everything. You can ace all the classroom stuff, but if you can't function in the actual hospital environment, you're just toast. And it's a super fast-paced environment, right? You've got outpatients coming in for routine chest x-rays, you've got ER patients rolling in on stretchers needing full trauma series, and you have to be incredibly efficient. But for me, because I literally cannot stop moving—like, I'll be pacing around the control booth, or constantly shifting my weight, or messing with the lead aprons while the supervising tech is trying to explain a specific protocol to me—it's actually starting to cause real problems. 

My supervisors pulled me into the office last week, and they were really serious about it. They told me that my behavior is actively disrupting the patient flow. Which... I mean, I guess I kind of see their point? Like, if I'm supposed to be setting up the wall bucky for a standing exam, but I've wandered over to the other side of the room to look at the monitors because I couldn't just stand there waiting for the patient to change into their gown, it does slow things down. And they said it makes teamwork a lot harder, too. The other techs feel like they constantly have to keep track of where I am or what I'm doing, instead of just trusting me to stay at my post and be ready for the next exposure. 

So, because of all that... they actually put me on a formal remediation plan. Yeah. An actual, documented remediation plan. It's this whole official process where I have to meet these specific behavioral goals every single week, basically proving to them that I can stay on task and not bounce off the walls during my clinical shifts. 

And honestly, doctor, I'm just... I'm really, really worried about it. This program is my whole life right now. I've worked so hard to get in, and I love the work, I really do. But if I don't get this under control, if I can't figure out how to just stand still and do the job exactly the way they need me to do it... it could actually cost me my place in the program. They could kick me out. And I just don't know what I'd do if that happened. So, yeah, I'm desperately trying to change how I act during my shifts, because the stakes are just so incredibly high, but it is taking every ounce of energy I have just to try and stand in one place.

Like, I’d have half the math problems done while everyone else was still getting their pencils out, but then I'd be up and walking around the room because I was done and bored. So, yeah, this definitely isn't a new thing. It was happening way, way before middle school, and definitely way before I ever started this radiology training. It’s just that now, in the clinical setting, the stakes feel higher, you know? But the actual feeling of needing to move? That’s been there since I was a little kid, just driving my elementary school teachers completely up the wall.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: I mean... when you say acting on impulse, what exactly do you mean? You absolutely cannot just do things without thinking about the consequences. You're dealing with ionizing radiation, you're dealing with patient safety, contrast protocols, all of that. If you don't think about the consequences of, say, forgetting to shield a patient, or setting your technical factors—like your kVp or mAs—way too high, you could actually really harm someone. I might be tapping my foot or pacing around the control room while I'm waiting for the tube to warm up, but I'm never just... pressing buttons on a whim or jumping into a procedure blindly. I always know exactly what I'm doing and what the result is going to be. \n\nEven outside of the hospital, like just hanging out with my friends or whatever, I'm not the guy who just, I don't know, jumps off a roof into a pool or spends all my tuition money on a whim because it sounded fun for five seconds. I definitely know what the outcome of a situation is going to be before I do something. So, yeah, I really wouldn't say I act without thinking. I just have a ton of physical energy while I'm doing the thinking, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Are your symptoms affecting your relationships with friends or family?\n\nPatient: Affecting my relationships? Um... I mean, not really? Not in a bad way, at least. Like, I wouldn't say my friends are mad at me or anything. We still hang out all the time. I mean, sure, if we're studying together for our physics exams—because radiographic physics is just brutal, by the way, trying to memorize all the inverse square law stuff and the anode heel effect—I'll be the one pacing around the library or tossing a highlighter up and down while they're just sitting there quietly reviewing their notes. But they're totally used to it by now. They just know that's how I operate. I just couldn't do it. You absolutely cannot just do things without thinking about the consequences. You're dealing with ionizing radiation, you're dealing with patient safety, contrast protocols, all of that. I might be tapping my foot or pacing around the control room while I'm waiting for the tube to warm up, but I'm never just... pressing buttons on a whim or jumping into a procedure blindly. I always know exactly what I'm doing and what the result is going to be. \n\nEven outside of the hospital, like just hanging out with my friends or whatever, I'm not the guy who just, I don't know, jumps off a roof into a pool or spends all my tuition money on a whim because it sounded fun for five seconds. I could recite the exact protocol we were doing right back to him. \n\nIt’s not my brain wandering off, you know? It’s just my body refusing to stay in standby mode. So, yeah, I really don't think it's an attention thing.
